analysis.one_liner: Phases out the legal exemption letting employers pay workers with disabilities below minimum wage.
analysis.headline: The bill to phase out subminimum wages for workers with disabilities died in committee without a vote in the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law has long allowed employers to get a special certificate letting them pay workers with disabilities less than the minimum wage — sometimes only a few dollars an hour. This bill would stop issuing new certificates, raise the allowed wage in steps over five years, then end the program entirely. To ease the change, it would give states and employers up to $200 million a year in grants to convert their operations so workers with disabilities hold regular jobs at regular pay in mainstream workplaces. The bill never received a hearing or vote; it sat in the Senate health committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers with disabilities currently employed under 14(c) certificates — often in segregated 'sheltered workshop' settings — would gain the legal right to at least the full federal or state minimum wage and pay equal to what coworkers without disabilities earn for the same work. Workers who have been underpaid for years gain back wages; people with disabilities gain access to mainstream jobs alongside nondisabled coworkers, backed by transition support services.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers with disabilities paid subminimum wages

how_it_helps.text: It bans the issuance of new 14(c) certificates and sunsets existing ones after five years, during which the legal wage floor for certificate holders rises in steps — 60% of minimum wage in year one up to the full minimum wage in year five.

It funds grants (up to $15 million per state over five years, $200k–$750k for individual employers) to help employers convert to paying workers with disabilities at least the full minimum wage and the customary rate for the same work.

It requires an independent evaluation of the transition and annual Wage and Hour reports on wages, hours, and transitions of certificate holders, plus an audit of at least 10% of certificate-holding employers in the first year.

analysis.who_pays: Employers holding 14(c) certificates — mostly nonprofit disability service providers running sheltered workshops and some for-profit contractors — would bear the cost of raising wages and restructuring their business models, softened by transition grants of up to $750,000 per entity. Taxpayers fund the grant program (authorized at $200 million per year for five years).
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers using subminimum-wage certificates; taxpayers fund transition

drawbacks.text: Employers currently paying subminimum wages would face a rising wage mandate (60% of minimum rising to 100% over five years), and some sheltered-workshop programs might close rather than transform, leaving some workers without the activity and structure those settings provided.
The transition depends on grants that are authorized but not guaranteed appropriations; if funding falls short, employers would face the wage mandate without the support the bill assumes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — ending a legal carve-out that lets employers pay workers with disabilities less than everyone else — is significant, and the bill pays the transition cost itself with five years of grants rather than dumping it on employers or workers. The honest drawback is risk: no one knows how many of these jobs survive as full-wage jobs, and the bill proceeds with the phase-out on a fixed clock regardless. Critics also note some families value the sheltered workshops. The five-year ramp and transition grants mitigate, but do not eliminate, that risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate HELP Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: S. 3238 was introduced in the Senate on November 18, 2021 by Senator Casey with Senator Daines as the Republican co-lead.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee; no further action is recorded.
The bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or action in the House, and expired with the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers holding 14(c) certificates keep the legal ability to pay workers with disabilities subminimum wages; the status quo for segregated, low-wage disability employment continued.

for.name: Sen. Robert Casey Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its push to phase out subminimum-wage certificates.

for.name: Sen. Steve Daines
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's Republican co-sponsor at introduction.

for.name: 6 of 48 Senate Democrats, 1 of 50 Senate Republicans, 1 of 2 Senate Independents

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on introduction and took no action — no markup, no hearing recorded, no report — leaving the bill to expire at the end of the 117th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democrat leading with one Republican and one Independent among eight cosponsors — but no committee or floor vote was ever taken, so no partisan division was recorded.

industries.industry: Sheltered workshops and 14(c) certificate holders (disability service providers)
industries.note: They would lose the legal ability to pay workers with disabilities below minimum wage, with transition grants cushioning the change over five years. This subminimum-wage arrangement is their labor cost structure, so they lose it.

industries.industry: Community-based disability employment and service providers
industries.note: Competitive integrated employers and providers of integrated support services would gain workers, referrals, and new grant funding as the model shifts away from segregated settings.

industries.industry: State Medicaid and disability service systems
industries.note: States would need to reorganize services around integrated employment and could eventually gain dedicated federal funding under a new Rehabilitation Act title if they complete the transition successfully.
